title: Full-length Reed–Solomon list decoding beyond Johnson
formal: Do there exist real constants \(\varepsilon,\rho\in(0,1)\) with \(\varepsilon<\sqrt{\rho}\), a constant \(K\ge1\), an integer \(c\ge1\), and infinitely many prime powers \(q\), such that for every function \(r:\mathbb F_q\to\mathbb F_q\), \[\left|\left\{f\in\mathbb F_q[X]:\deg f\le\lfloor\rho q\rfloor,\;\bigl|\{x\in\mathbb F_q:f(x)=r(x)\}\bigr|>\varepsilon q\right\}\right|\le Kq^c?\] The zero polynomial is included among the degree-bounded polynomials. All four constants are fixed independently of \(q\) and of the received function \(r\). This is the combinatorial full-length Reed–Solomon question from Open Problem 5.20, without a requirement for an efficient decoding algorithm.
why: Reed–Solomon codes are a central algebraic code family, and their list size expresses an intrinsic information limit even when computation is unrestricted. The full-length requirement fixes the evaluation set completely. Determining whether any constant-rate infinite family surpasses the Johnson threshold would resolve a basic distinction between this rigid algebraic family and the punctured variants for which capacity results are known.
status_note: The precise target is open in Vadhan’s 2012 source. The checked 2025 primary papers explicitly distinguish full-length codes from the punctured families covered by their positive results. Bounded searches through 2026-09-15 found no proof or refutation of the displayed full-length existence statement. This review does not claim that all later parameter regimes or proofs were exhaustively checked.

progress.text: Vadhan’s Open Problem 5.20 records the precise fixed-parameter, infinite-sequence full-length combinatorial question.
The capacity results of Brakensiek, Gopi and Makam and subsequent alphabet-size improvements concern randomly punctured Reed–Solomon codes, as reviewed in the 2025 joint paper.
Li and Shagrithaya prove list-recovery capacity results for random code families and distinguish their punctured-code guarantees from full-length list-recovery obstructions.

sentences: The question asks whether some infinite family of full-length Reed–Solomon codes has polynomially bounded lists beyond the Johnson threshold.
The code evaluates every polynomial of degree at most a fixed fraction of the field size at every field element.
One fixed pair of rate and agreement constants and one polynomial list bound must work for every received word along infinitely many field sizes.
This is an information-theoretic existence question and does not demand an efficient decoding algorithm.
Recent capacity theorems for randomly punctured codes and lower bounds for list recovery have different quantifiers or models and do not settle this target.

definitions: A prime power is \(q=p^m\), where \(p\) is a prime and \(m\ge1\) is an integer; the characteristic may vary along the infinite set. The field \(\mathbb F_q\) has exactly \(q\) elements. Let \(d=\lfloor\rho q\rfloor\). The code consists of evaluations of all formal polynomials \(\sum_{j=0}^{d}a_jX^j\), with \(a_j\in\mathbb F_q\), at every element of the field. Its block length and alphabet size are both \(q\), its dimension is \(d+1\), and its rate is \((d+1)/q\), which tends to \(\rho\) as \(q\) grows. Because \(d<q\), distinct allowed polynomials give distinct codewords. Coordinates are indexed by field elements, so no ordering choice matters. A received word is an arbitrary function on this entire field and need not be a low-degree polynomial. Its agreement fraction with a codeword is \(q^{-1}|\{x:f(x)=r(x)\}|\); the normalized Hamming distance is one minus this fraction. The displayed list uses strict agreement \(>\varepsilon\), equivalently distance \(<1-\varepsilon\), following the source’s LIST convention. Thus a boundary with exactly \(\varepsilon q\) agreements is excluded. The list is a set of distinct polynomials, not a list with repetitions. The polynomial bound \(Kq^c\) is uniform over all received words and all selected field sizes. Infinitely many prime powers means an unbounded set of distinct values of \(q\); it does not mean every sufficiently large prime power. No efficient method for selecting that infinite set, constructing field representations, finding the list, or encoding its members is required. The evaluation set may not be punctured or replaced by a random proper subset; neither folded symbols, derivatives, restricted message spaces, nor an average over received words is part of the target.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the displayed existence statement or its negation. A positive proof must establish one fixed admissible pair \((\varepsilon,\rho)\), one polynomial list bound and infinitely many field sizes, and the bound must hold for every received word at each of those sizes. It need not supply a decoder. A negative proof must show that for every admissible pair and every \(K\ge1,c\ge1\), only finitely many prime powers have the uniform list bound. Equivalently, beyond a threshold depending on those constants, every prime power must admit some received word with more than \(Kq^c\) qualifying polynomials. Hard instances for only one rate, one characteristic, or an infinite but not exhaustive subsequence do not by themselves refute the existence statement. Results for randomly punctured codes, list recovery with multiple candidate symbols per coordinate, or only algorithmic hardness do not settle this combinatorial full-length target.

context_blocks.text: Vadhan’s Construction 5.14 defines the full-length code by evaluating every degree-at-most-\(d\) polynomial over the entire field. Definition 5.18 uses strict agreement, and Open Problem 5.20 asks for fixed \(\varepsilon<\sqrt{\rho}\) with degree \(\lfloor\rho q\rfloor\) and polynomial list size along an infinite sequence. The rate convention differs slightly from writing the degree as the dimension.

The Johnson bound and the algorithms recalled in the textbook provide the familiar square-root threshold. The open question asks whether some fixed constant parameters can do strictly better at the level of list cardinalities, including with inefficient decoding.

The 2025 joint journal paper of Alrabiah, Guo, Guruswami, Li and Zhang establishes capacity results for randomly punctured Reed–Solomon codes over fields whose sizes are linear in the block length. “Linear-sized” does not mean equal to the block length. Theorem 1.1 explicitly requires a field size strictly greater than the block length when the dimension is positive, so it does not apply to the full-length codes here.

That paper’s introduction distinguishes combinatorial obstructions for some full-length parameter regimes, due to Ben-Sasson, Kopparty and Radhakrishnan, from the later positive puncturing results. A restriction in some regimes does not refute the present existence quantifiers over parameters and infinitely many field sizes.

Li and Shagrithaya’s 2025 paper addresses list recovery, where each received coordinate may specify several acceptable symbols. Its discussion of full-length Reed–Solomon lower bounds concerns that stronger task. Ordinary list decoding here has exactly one received symbol at each coordinate.
